verdict: The methodology is genuinely better than most published browser latency work — three independent clocks per keystroke, a hard keys-pressed == keydowns-in-trace == keys-resolved assertion, a real 10,062-word document, p99 everywhere, and the vsync-clock correction validated against a real panel to within 0.6 ms on frame commit — and §9 is an unusually honest list of what the numbers are not. But the one claim that actually touches the bar, ≈32 ms keyboard-to-photon, is a p50 from an earlier build measured once on glass with a known double-probe bug, plus two constants cited from Fatin rather than measured; that same session's end-of-draft regime shows 48.5 ms p99, which is the VS Code bracket, and the report quotes the better regime. Meanwhile the bench types nothing but lowercase letters and spaces, so it never presses Enter or Backspace — precisely the line-count-changing path that core.js's render() gives a more expensive branch and that round 1 chose not to optimise — and there is no throttled-CPU run despite the doc-size table already showing 12.9 ms of main-thread work per key at 55k words. App-internal cost (2.94 ms to committed frame, 4.23 p50 / 6.14 p99 with the clock off) does beat the ≤5 ms bar and that part I believe; the keyboard-to-photon headline is a tie dressed as a win, and it is resting on the weakest run in the set.

builderNote: Rewrote tools/latency.mjs into an honest per-keystroke bench: Chrome's own unrounded EventTiming trace records (hardware timestamp → presentation feedback of the frame that carried it), cross-checked by an in-page rAF/MessageChannel probe and de-nested main-thread accounting, over a real 10,062-word Alice document (plus 2k/27k/55k for scaling), five typing regimes, caret scrolled on screen, warm-ups discarded, and every keystroke asserted for (the old bench silently measured 62 of 150 keys); it also fixes the trap that makes browser latency numbers lie — headless only ticks when something animates, worth ~6 ms, so the bench now keeps a 1 px composited animation running to model a 60 Hz panel and reports "application cost" separately. Result on the committed build: keystroke → presented frame p50 10.8 / p95 18.5 / p99 19.1 ms on a 60 Hz clock (4.2 / 6.1 as pure app cost, 13.8 / 29.1 measured on a real 60 Hz panel), 4.9 ms of main thread per keystroke of which 0.85 ms is Quill's own code, document on screen 100 ms after navigation and 395–511 ms through the new bin/quill launcher — an estimated ≈32 ms keyboard-to-photon, the Sublime/TextEdit bracket. Four perf-only core.js changes (ResizeObserver instead of a forced layout per keystroke, one selection notification instead of three, writes before reads, no attribute storm) A/B'd on twin snapshot servers: 4.84 → 4.17 ms main thread per key, p99 9.01 → 5.93 ms, 12.07 → 6.08 layout-reading DOM calls.
secondary: Only lowercase letters and spaces are ever typed. tools/latency.mjs types from one fixed sample sentence ('the quick brown fox...') via page.keyboard.press — no Enter, no Backspace, no punctuation, no Markdown-triggering characters (* _ # `), no paste, no undo, no select-and-replace, no IME. This is not incidental: app/js/core.js render() skips the renumber loop entirely when `newN !== oldN` is false, so the bench exclusively exercises the cheap path that round 1 optimised and never once touches the path round 1 deliberately left in place. Pressing Enter in the 3,285-line doc52k walks every line element below the caret; typing a backtick can invalidate lineCtx fence state for the rest of the document via recomputeCtx. Both are zero-data.

Startup '100 ms, median of 12 cold loads' is not cold. measure() calls browser.newContext() in a live browser: warm browser process, warm GPU process, warm system fonts, warm V8 compile cache, warm localhost server, no process spawn. The genuinely cold number is n=2 (395 and 511 ms) on a WARM profile; bin/quill --fresh exists and was never run, so true first-run startup is unmeasured. The progress tile also labels 100 ms as 'Startup → editor ready' when editor-ready is 71 ms and 100 ms is FCP.

No degraded-hardware run at all. i5-13600K, 20 threads, load 0.61, nothing else on the machine. Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate is one CDP call and there is no 2×/4× run anywhere. §9's claim that 'the number that scales is main-thread work per keystroke' is asserted, not demonstrated — and §6 already shows 12.9 ms/key at 55k words, so a 4× slower machine blows one 60 Hz frame on a document a quarter that size.

p99 from a single n=300 run is the 3rd-worst sample of 300, with no repeated sessions and no confidence interval. Every regime was run exactly once. Startup reports sd across 12 runs; typing reports nothing about run-to-run variance, which is the only thing that makes a p99 meaningful.

~304 frames marked STATE_DROPPED_affecting_smoothness per 300 keystrokes in every paced headless regime — roughly one dropped frame per keystroke — recorded in the JSON and then declined in §9 as an artefact of the bench's own 1 px clock animation. That is a plausible explanation, not a demonstrated one; a compositor-only opacity animation should not need a main-thread update, so ~1 missed deadline per keystroke wants a root cause before it is dismissed.

The headline pairing in dev/progress/latency.json and the progress-page tiles is apples-to-oranges. 'Keystroke → paint p50 10.82 ms' sits next to 'Bar 32.5 ms' and reads as 3× better than Sublime. 10.82 is app+compositor with no keyboard and no panel; 32.5 is key-switch-to-photon. latency-report.md §4.1 maps the three bars correctly and honestly; the machine-readable summary and the tiles a reader actually sees do not.

The ≤5 ms app-internal bar is only cleared on the 10k document with focus off. Focus: Sentence is 5.43 ms main-thread busy (over the bar), 26k words is 7.6 ms, 55k is 12.9 ms. The report's '55,000-word manuscript still fits a keystroke inside one 60 Hz frame' is a main-thread-busy claim; app-cost p99 there is 15.2 ms with the display clock OFF, so on a real 60 Hz panel that document is ~21 ms p50 / ~27 ms p99 — over a frame, not inside one.

Sustained-session behaviour is unmeasured. Each regime is ~27 s of typing. No long-session run, no GC/memory growth data, and no accounting for the document autosave write (53 KB to localStorage, in files.js) — main_thread_us_per_keystroke attributes textInput, the input handler and style/layout/paint, but a periodic multi-millisecond storage flush would be under-sampled by a 300-key window and does not appear in the breakdown.

saturation_stress's headline p50 of 10.02 ms is close to meaningless and is still tabulated alongside the others: only 32 frames were PRESENTED_ALL for 300 keystrokes, i.e. ~10 keys per frame, so per-key presented latency is measuring frame sharing rather than responsiveness. §9 says this and gives the honest 77 ms p99 queue figure from the in-page probe, but the results table in §4 still shows it as a 10.0 ms row.
